items.title: A Clarification
items.summary:
I made a point in this post inelegantly in a way that was easy to misunderstand, so I’d like to clarify it.

I didn’t mean that we need to tolerate brilliant homophobic jerks in the lab so that we can have scientific progress. Although there are famous counterexamples, most of the best scientists I’ve met are unusually nice, open-minded people. Generally I expect that labs that don’t tolerate jerks will produce more impressive results than the ones that do, and choosing not to employ jerks is a good idea—jerks usually reduce the net output of organizations.

What I meant is simply that we need, as a society, to tolerate controversial ideas. The biggest new scientific ideas, and the most important changes to society, both start as extremely unpopular ideas.

It was literally heretical, not so long ago, to say that it was ok to be gay—the Bible has a different viewpoint. In a society where we don’t allow challenges to the orthodoxy, gay rights would not have happened.

We need to allow free speech because sometimes society is wrong—we needed people to be able to say “gay people are ok” at a time when “gay people are evil” was the consensus opinion.

It’s probably impossible to design a simple set of rules that will always allow the right speech and not the wrong speech (although I am sure that in this particular case, it is wrong that gay people in some places still fear for their safety.)

So we agree as a society that people are allowed to say controversial things, and that free speech goes both ways. Much of the time people use that privilege to be jerks, and we can, should, and do point out why their bigotry is bad. Sometimes they use it to say that people deserve more rights, or that the solar system works in a different way from what the church says—and sometimes we collectively listen.

Over time, this system produces a more and more just world, which says something really good about people as a whole.

I wish we could figure out a way to just never allow hate, discrimination, and bigotry and always allow debate on controversial but important ideas. If that were possible, I’d support it. The distinction is usually clear, but the exceptions are sometimes critically important. Figuring out exactly where to draw the line is really hard.

Generations before us believed a lot of things we now believe (correctly, in my opinion) to be unethical or wrong. Future generations will think a lot of things we believe today are unethical or wrong.

For example, today it is pretty unpopular to say “anyone who eats meat is unethical”. But this is easily a stance I could imagine being commonplace in 50 years, because of evolving views on animal rights, impact on the planet, and availability of lab-grown replacements. Perhaps even the arrival of AI makes us think differently about being ok eating other beings just because they’re much less smart/emotionally sophisticated than we are.

The last time I tried to discuss this with someone, he said something like: “Banning eating meat would be infringing on my rights, this is not up for discussion.”

I expect the fact that we let people live in poverty is also something that future generations will consider an absolute moral failing. I could go on with a long list of other ideas, and I’m sure I can’t even think of some of the most important ones.

The point I most wanted to make is that is that it’s dangerous to just ban discussion of topics we find offensive, like what happened yesterday.

items.title: E Pur Si Muove
items.summary:
Earlier this year, I noticed something in China that really surprised me. I realized I felt more comfortable discussing controversial ideas in Beijing than in San Francisco. I didn’t feel completely comfortable—this was China, after all—just more comfortable than at home.

That showed me just how bad things have become, and how much things have changed since I first got started here in 2005.

It seems easier to accidentally speak heresies in San Francisco every year. Debating a controversial idea, even if you 95% agree with the consensus side, seems ill-advised.

This will be very bad for startups in the Bay Area.

Restricting speech leads to restricting ideas and therefore restricted innovation—the most successful societies have generally been the most open ones. Usually mainstream ideas are right and heterodox ideas are wrong, but the true and unpopular ideas are what drive the world forward. Also, smart people tend to have an allergic reaction to the restriction of ideas, and I’m now seeing many of the smartest people I know move elsewhere.

It is bad for all of us when people can’t say that the world is a sphere, that evolution is real, or that the sun is at the center of the solar system.

More recently, I’ve seen credible people working on ideas like pharmaceuticals for intelligence augmentation, genetic engineering, and radical life extension leave San Francisco because they found the reaction to their work to be so toxic. “If people live a lot longer it will be disastrous for the environment, so people working on this must be really unethical” was a memorable quote I heard this year.

To get the really good ideas, we need to tolerate really bad and wacky ideas too. In addition to the work Newton is best known for, he also studied alchemy (the British authorities banned work on this because they feared the devaluation of gold) and considered himself to be someone specially chosen by the almighty for the task of decoding Biblical scripture.

You can’t tell which seemingly wacky ideas are going to turn out to be right, and nearly all ideas that turn out to be great breakthroughs start out sounding like terrible ideas. So if you want a culture that innovates, you can’t have a culture where you allow the concept of heresy—if you allow the concept at all, it tends to spread. When we move from strenuous debate about ideas to casting the people behind the ideas as heretics, we gradually stop debate on all controversial ideas.

This is uncomfortable, but it’s possible we have to allow people to say disparaging things about gay people if we want them to be able to say novel things about physics. [1] Of course we can and should say that ideas are mistaken, but we can’t just call the person a heretic. We need to debate the actual idea.

Political correctness often comes from a good place—I think we should all be willing to make accommodations to treat others well. But too often it ends up being used as a club for something orthogonal to protecting actual victims. The best ideas are barely possible to express at all, and if you’re constantly thinking about how everything you say might be misinterpreted, you won’t let the best ideas get past the fragment stage.

I don’t know who Satoshi is, but I’m skeptical that he, she, or they would have been able to come up with the idea for bitcoin immersed in the current culture of San Francisco—it would have seemed too crazy and too dangerous, with too many ways to go wrong. If SpaceX started in San Francisco in 2017, I assume they would have been attacked for focusing on problems of the 1%, or for doing something the government had already decided was too hard. I can picture Galileo looking up at the sky and whispering “E pur si muove” here today.


Followup: A Clarification



[1] I am less worried that letting some people on the internet say things like “gay people are evil” is going to convince reasonable people that such a statement is true than I fear losing the opposite—we needed people to be free to say "gay people are ok" to make the progress we've made, even though it was not a generally acceptable thought several decades ago.

In fact, the only ideas I’m afraid of letting people say are the ones that I think may be true and that I don’t like. But I accept that censorship is not going to make the world be the way I wish it were.

items.title: The Merge
items.summary:
A popular topic in Silicon Valley is talking about what year humans and machines will merge (or, if not, what year humans will get surpassed by rapidly improving AI or a genetically enhanced species). Most guesses seem to be between 2025 and 2075.

People used to call this the singularity; now it feels uncomfortable and real enough that many seem to avoid naming it at all.

Perhaps another reason people stopped using the word “singularity” is that it implies a single moment in time, and it now looks like the merge is going to be a gradual process. And gradual processes are hard to notice.

I believe the merge has already started, and we are a few years in. Our phones control us and tell us what to do when; social media feeds determine how we feel; search engines decide what we think.

The algorithms that make all this happen are no longer understood by any one person. They optimize for what their creators tell them to optimize for, but in ways that no human could figure out — they are what today seems like sophisticated AI, and tomorrow will seem like child’s play. And they’re extremely effective — at least speaking for myself, I have a very hard time resisting what the algorithms want me to do. Until I made a real effort to combat it, I found myself getting extremely addicted to the internet. [1]

We are already in the phase of co-evolution — the AIs affect, effect, and infect us, and then we improve the AI. We build more computing power and run the AI on it, and it figures out how to build even better chips.

This probably cannot be stopped. As we have learned, scientific advancement eventually happens if the laws of physics do not prevent it.

More important than that, unless we destroy ourselves first, superhuman AI is going to happen, genetic enhancement is going to happen, and brain-machine interfaces are going to happen. It is a failure of human imagination and human arrogance to assume that we will never build things smarter than ourselves.

Our self-worth is so based on our intelligence that we believe it must be singular and not slightly higher than all the other animals on a continuum. Perhaps the AI will feel the same way and note that differences between us and bonobos are barely worth discussing.

The merge can take a lot of forms: We could plug electrodes into our brains, or we could all just become really close friends with a chatbot. But I think a merge is probably our best-case scenario. If two different species both want the same thing and only one can have it—in this case, to be the dominant species on the planet and beyond—they are going to have conflict. We should all want one team where all members care about the well-being of everyone else.

Although the merge has already begun, it’s going to get a lot weirder. We will be the first species ever to design our own descendants. My guess is that we can either be the biological bootloader for digital intelligence and then fade into an evolutionary tree branch, or we can figure out what a successful merge looks like.

It’s probably going to happen sooner than most people think. Hardware is improving at an exponential rate—the most surprising thing I’ve learned working on OpenAI is just how correlated increasing computing power and AI breakthroughs are—and the number of smart people working on AI is increasing exponentially as well. Double exponential functions get away from you fast.

It would be good for the entire world to start taking this a lot more seriously now. Worldwide coordination doesn’t happen quickly, and we need it for this.



[1] I believe attention hacking is going to be the sugar epidemic of this generation. I can feel the changes in my own life — I can still wistfully remember when I had an attention span. My friends’ young children don’t even know that’s something they should miss. I am angry and unhappy more often, but I channel it into productive change less often, instead chasing the dual dopamine hits of likes and outrage.

(Cross-posted from https://medium.com/wordsthatmatter/merge-now-430c6d89d1fe to here for consistency; thanks to Medium for inviting me to write this!)

items.title: DoorDash and Thrive Go Shopping
items.summary:
Get your deals in while ya still can, folks. And clearly, there are relative bargains to be had. 

DoorDash CEO Tony Xu gets what I’m talking about. On Thursday, Xu finally picked up Instacart, with Xu’s company saying it would pay about $17 billion for the grocery-delivery business. Over on X, Instacart founder Apoorva Mehta sent up a resounding huzzah, saying he and Xu had long discussed such a transaction. That wasn’t news to readers of The Information: We reported on talks between DoorDash and Instacart back in 2021.

At one point in 2021, DoorDash was considering buying Instacart for more than $40 billion. By waiting, Xu obviously saved himself a bunch of money and avoided the ridiculous markups that were attached to pandemic-era darlings like Instacart. Sure, its prospects seemed rosier back then, when we were regarding physical grocery stores as potentially lethal germ pools, but Xu doesn’t seem to be getting a total lemon. In the third quarter, Instacart sales grew 17%, and it generated a decent amount of cash in that time—more than $300 million, a 13% increase. 

The sale to Xu does solve Instacart’s leadership problem: It had looked rather rudderless since Fidji Simo left the CEO role for OpenAI in 2025. Still, Xu will need to figure out how to handle the fierce competition for online grocery sales, a battle that includes Walmart and Amazon (more on the latter company below). 

One thing that held Xu up in 2021 was concern about the Biden administration. According to Valida’s reporting, Xu figured DoorDash wouldn’t get an Instacart acquisition past Biden regulators, who, of course, were trying their hardest to squelch corporate mergers and acquisitions. Those days of dealmaking famine have given way to a time of great feasting: The Trump White House has been, uh, lenient with regulatory approval. It could all shift once again after the midterms. With Democrats seemingly set to retake Congress next week, and President Donald Trump enjoying the same popularity as a DoorDasher who shows up with a carton of broken eggs, the idea of a liberal in the White House after 2028 seems a lot more plausible than it did even a few months ago. 

The prospect of a Democrat in the White House will spur plenty more M&A to happen sooner rather than later. I get it. Judging by the words of liberal standard-bearer Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, the left’s attitude toward mergers does not seem to have changed much since President Joe Biden creaked out of office. On Thursday, Mamdani criticized the DoorDash-Instacart deal, saying in a post on X that such moves often bring higher prices for consumers and “harsher exploitation” for workers. 

In addition to politics, M&A sure seems likely to keep humming for the simple reason that there are plenty of other Instacarts out there—businesses that haven’t fared well since their pandemic glory days. Zoom, Duolingo, Coursera: I could go on. I would’ve put Bumble right there, too, had it not already limped into the welcoming arms of investor Ravi Gupta several weeks ago. (Gupta bought Bumble for about $6 a share; Bumble once traded hands at more than $75.) Other M&A action seems like it’ll be driven by the chance to spruce up an aging business with AI, which I imagine is the motivating force behind the other deal announced on Thursday: Josh Kushner’s $7.6 billion purchase of ADT, maker of home security systems, through the newly formed Thrive Holdings, an offshoot of his Thrive Capital. 

Another reason that I’m going on and on about M&A today is because I listened to what Goldman Sachs’ Kim Posnett, the bank’s global co-head of investment banking, had to say about the topic at our WTF conference earlier this week. By the sounds of things, her direct messages are cluttered with missives from deal-hungry CEOs. “They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape. CEOs are leaning in right now—they wanna make big strategic bets,” she said. “We’re optimistic.” Still, as she pointed out, “things change quickly.”—Abram Brown

Amazon’s Agita

If there’s a lesson in the earnings reports from Amazon and Google over the past couple of days, it’s that investors are more in the mood to focus on the companies’ blemishes rather than the strong performance of their cloud units. 

On Thursday, Amazon said revenues from its Amazon Web Services unit had surged 39% to $45.98 billion, its strongest growth rate in nearly four years. That was an impressive feat given that second-quarter AWS revenues grew at a record 37%. And if that wasn’t enough, Amazon CEO Andy Jassy forecast AWS growth rates of over 40% in 2027 and 2028. 

On a call with analysts, Jassy went even further and predicted that AWS could be one of two businesses for Amazon with $1 trillion a year revenue within the next five to 10 years (the other is its stores business—Amazon-speak for its e-commerce business and everything else, excluding AWS).

But, it turns out, that was not enough for investors, many of whom are increasingly on edge about whether tech giants will see a sustainable payoff from the colossal amounts of money they’re spending on AI. Amazon shares dropped more than 6% in after-hours trading. 

The company’s total net sales were $201.9 billion, up 12%, while its net income was $20.7 billion, down slightly from a year earlier, when it had a pre-tax gain of $9.5 billion from its investment in Anthropic. Even though Amazon’s numbers were within its own forecasts, Wall Street analysts were expecting slightly better results. The company left its estimate for its 2026 capital expenditures—most of which is going to its spending on data centers—unchanged at $220 billion.

Google had a similar experience today. Investors punished its stock, sending it down 12%. It appears they were more keen to focus on the bad in its Wednesday earnings report (sluggish revenue growth in its core search advertising business) rather than the good (a doubling of Google Cloud revenues). The AI glass seems to be half full for many investors right now.—Nick Wingfield

In Other News

  • U.S. intelligence agencies found that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was the target of a Chinese spy.
  • Coinbase’s latest earnings report showed the company had returned to profitability in the third quarter while sales had declined, underscoring how closely tied it remains to cryptocurrencies—despite a push to boost growth through new areas like prediction markets.
  • Intel shares plunged nearly 20% in after-hours trading after the firm said a slump in its business for PC processors would continue.
  • A suspected hack of Binance, a major crypto exchange, could involve billions of dollars.

items.title: Nvidia Moves to Backstop a Cloud Provider’s $45 Billion Anthropic Project
items.summary:
Nvidia is in talks to provide Nscale, a young AI cloud provider, with billions of dollars in credit guarantees for debt to develop a 460-megawatt data center that Anthropic plans to use, according to people with knowledge of the deal discussions.

The deal is not yet signed, and terms could change. But it is another example of how Nvidia has continued to signal its financial support of so-called neoclouds like Nscale, CoreWeave and Firmus, which have faced pressure from investors because of the debt those companies have raised will still need to raise to develop specialized data centers for AI.

items.title: Why Private Equity’s Fundraising Divide Is Pushing Newcomers Toward AI
items.summary:
Private equity fundraising has become a story of haves and have-nots, as a prolonged slowdown in firms selling portfolio companies leaves investors with less cash to put into new funds. Giants like Blackstone are still raking in capital while some smaller firms struggle to attract investors, forcing newcomers to find creative ways to stand out. 

Some firms are betting that they can differentiate themselves by pushing AI to transform companies and boost returns. While larger private equity firms are also using AI across portfolio companies, such newcomers are making it central to their investment strategies. 

That includes Aldaron, which has dubbed itself a “transformation equity firm.” The 12-person firm uses an in-house team of engineers to deploy AI at the companies it acquires, though it emphasizes that its goal is to use the technology to grow businesses without cutting jobs. 

In a challenging private equity fundraising environment, “the core message that resonated with people is this transformation equity story,” said Aldaron Partners co-founder Evan Mendez, who previously worked on technology investments at the Carlyle Group. He said the firm has a “hybrid group of investors and engineers that source a company, build the thesis together, cocreate a vision with the management team, underwrite the deal, put their own capital into the deal, and then embed into that company to go execute the road map.”

Aldaron completed its first acquisition in March, buying a majority stake in Oak Point Partners, an investment firm that buys remnant assets like IP and recovery claims. Aldaron funded that deal with money from early investors, some of which also made direct investments in Oak Point. Aldaron continued raising money afterward, closing its first fund in October with $884 million from outside investors and more than $950 million in total including the coinvestments, Mendez said.

The broader fundraising squeeze comes amid a yearslong slump in sales and initial public offerings of private equity–backed companies, leaving many firms with holdings they picked up in the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. Private equity firms are sitting on nearly 4,600 U.S. companies they’ve owned for at least five years, according to an August PitchBook report, longer than the industry’s typical three- to five-year holding period. That means less cash is returning to the pension funds, endowments and other investors, known as limited partners, leaving them with less money to commit to new funds. 

The biggest private equity firms often have an edge in competing for fresh capital thanks to their long track records, along with their sizable sales teams that allow them to reach various pools of capital including wealthy individual investors. Smaller fund managers, particularly those that are trying to raise their second or third funds after struggling to return money to investors, could be squeezed out entirely. 

“We expect many managers to exit the market, and we are already seeing this as fundraising becomes more challenging,” said Mitchell Mansfield, a managing director at Kroll and global head of fund solutions, which advises fund managers on restructuring and winding down funds. 

To be sure, leaning into AI is just one way smaller private equity firms are finding ways to distinguish themselves. Some are narrowing their focus to a particular sector rather than competing with funds that invest across industries. They can also offer investors more attractive terms, such as opportunities to coinvest in deals, often with lower fees. Fund managers can also put more of their own money into investments. 

Broadwing Capital Management, for instance, started buying companies before completing its first institutional fundraising, betting that an existing portfolio would help win over investors. “It’s a lot easier to talk about an investment with folks than about the theory of a new firm,” said co-founder and managing partner Eliot Kerlin, who launched Broadwing after 15 years at middle-market private equity firm Insight Equity. 

Broadwing, which focuses on manufacturing, industrial services and distribution businesses, launched in 2022 and made its first three acquisitions using money from outside investors and some of the founders’ own capital before hiring a placement agent to raise a larger fund. The firm structured its early investments so they could become part of a growing fund as Broadwing raised more money. The strategy paid off—Broadwing closed its $440 million inaugural fund this August, surpassing its fundraising goal by $90 million. By then it already owned six companies. 

Goldman Sachs Says CEOs Are ‘Leaning In’ on Strategic M&A

Strategic megadeals are dominating the tech mergers and acquisitions landscape right now, Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. That will likely continue, Posnett said, and the bank has a robust pipeline of deal talks across the board.

“They’re talking about really big deals, industry consolidation. They’re talking about M&A to bridge strategic gaps. They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape,” she said. 

“CEOs are leaning in right now and they want to make big strategic bets,” she said, noting that there’s “a ton of” strategic activity in tech specifically. Posnett’s comments came ahead of DoorDash’s Thursday announcement of a $17 billion deal to buy Instacart. (The Information was first to report last week that Instacart was in sale talks.)

The broader fundraising squeeze comes amid a yearslong slump in sales and initial public offerings of private equity–backed companies, leaving many firms with holdings they picked up in the low-interest-rate years of 2020 and 2021. Private equity firms are sitting on nearly 4,600 U.S. companies they’ve owned for at least five years, according to an August PitchBook report, longer than the industry’s typical three- to five-year holding period. That means less cash is returning to the pension funds, endowments and other investors, known as limited partners, leaving them with less money to commit to new funds. 

The biggest private equity firms often have an edge in competing for fresh capital thanks to their long track records, along with their sizable sales teams that allow them to reach various pools of capital including wealthy individual investors. Smaller fund managers, particularly those that are trying to raise their second or third funds after struggling to return money to investors, could be squeezed out entirely. 

“We expect many managers to exit the market, and we are already seeing this as fundraising becomes more challenging,” said Mitchell Mansfield, a managing director at Kroll and global head of fund solutions, which advises fund managers on restructuring and winding down funds. 

To be sure, leaning into AI is just one way smaller private equity firms are finding ways to distinguish themselves. Some are narrowing their focus to a particular sector rather than competing with funds that invest across industries. They can also offer investors more attractive terms, such as opportunities to coinvest in deals, often with lower fees. Fund managers can also put more of their own money into investments. 

Broadwing Capital Management, for instance, started buying companies before completing its first institutional fundraising, betting that an existing portfolio would help win over investors. “It’s a lot easier to talk about an investment with folks than about the theory of a new firm,” said co-founder and managing partner Eliot Kerlin, who launched Broadwing after 15 years at middle-market private equity firm Insight Equity. 

Broadwing, which focuses on manufacturing, industrial services and distribution businesses, launched in 2022 and made its first three acquisitions using money from outside investors and some of the founders’ own capital before hiring a placement agent to raise a larger fund. The firm structured its early investments so they could become part of a growing fund as Broadwing raised more money. The strategy paid off—Broadwing closed its $440 million inaugural fund this August, surpassing its fundraising goal by $90 million. By then it already owned six companies. 

Goldman Sachs Says CEOs Are ‘Leaning In’ on Strategic M&A

Strategic megadeals are dominating the tech mergers and acquisitions landscape right now, Kim Posnett, Goldman Sachs’ global co-head of investment banking, said at The Information’s WTF Summit on Tuesday. That will likely continue, Posnett said, and the bank has a robust pipeline of deal talks across the board.

“They’re talking about really big deals, industry consolidation. They’re talking about M&A to bridge strategic gaps. They’re talking about M&A to drive growth. They’re talking about M&A to help reposition themselves in this new AI landscape,” she said. 

“CEOs are leaning in right now and they want to make big strategic bets,” she said, noting that there’s “a ton of” strategic activity in tech specifically. Posnett’s comments came ahead of DoorDash’s Thursday announcement of a $17 billion deal to buy Instacart. (The Information was first to report last week that Instacart was in sale talks.)

items.title: ‘Skeptical’ Lawyers Highlight Growing Pains of AI Agents
items.summary:
As Anthropic correctly pointed out in its initial public offering filing, business use of AI is in its infancy. Many other corporate executives say it will take some time for white-collar workers, especially those who aren’t software engineers, to use the latest tools effectively.

For example, White & Case, a large global law firm with more than 2,000 lawyers, is “having to hold back” its rollout of one of the newest legal assistants made by AI startup Legora because lawyers are hesitant about using so-called AI agents, said Isabel Parker, the law firm’s chief innovation officer. 

A gradual rollout will ensure lawyers feel confident in using the new agent, which can handle more complex legal work than the AI agent from Legora that lawyers currently use for tasks such as analyzing and summarizing documents and generating ideas, she said. Unlike simpler chatbots, AI agents can take multiple actions on behalf of the user.

Lawyers “are not the kind of people that easily lend themselves to using AI,” she told The Information’s Laura Mandaro during the WTF Summit, a gathering of senior women leaders in tech and finance. They’re “skeptical, they‘re time-poor, they’re risk averse, and they have a very strong conviction that their expertise is very artisanal...This technology comes along and it's a threat to everything they worked for.” 

Legora, a fast-growing app privately valued at roughly $9 billion, aims to automate legal work such as reviewing contracts and drafting documents—the kind of paperwork that needs to be error-free. In an email, Parker said White & Case is investing “significant amounts” in AI tools and that 90% of the firm’s staff uses Legora’s products to some extent. In some cases, using the products can save them as much as 80% of the time it took to manually perform tasks, she said.

Legora’s vice president of engagement, Jillian Burnett, said at the same event that the rapid pace of AI development means that lawyers must constantly learn new tools, which can wear them out.

“We’re working with a very skeptical [lawyer] client base overall, a very busy client base. And when they‘re already having to sit through trainings, different tools...lawyers aren’t necessarily going to want to give you more of their billable time to learn something new,” Burnett told Mandaro at the event.

She said Legora “didn't appreciate that fatigue enough” as a challenge to getting customers to use its tools. Legora has worked to address this by sending its staff to work with lawyers to show how the products can be “hyper-relevant” to their work.

Despite that resistance, Legora seems to be doing all right, and recently said it crossed $200 million in annualized recurring revenue. That implies it generates more than $16 million per month in revenue.

What is forcing change on White & Case lawyers is their clients. Parker said clients routinely ask the firm how it’s using new technologies to speed up work and how it can pass that “value” or new efficiencies to the clients. Now that both White & Case and the in-house legal teams of its clients often use the same AI apps and tools, “there’s nowhere to hide,” she said.

“One thing that cuts through any change fatigue in a lawyer is the client saying, ‘I want this done. Show me how you've been using this [AI tool],’” she said. 

In some cases, though, firms may intentionally slow AI use among junior employees to make sure they learn basic skills. For example, Parker said her firm is considering “sacrificing some efficiency” from AI so its junior lawyers can learn to do their work manually before adopting agents that can automate more difficult tasks such as Legora’s Agent Pro. 

“Most planes are flown by autopilot now...but you need to make sure that whoever's...in the cockpit does know how to fly a plane,” she said.

items.title: Solving for AI’s power problem
items.summary:
The AI race has long been defined by how quickly firms can stand up GPUs. Now, Elon Musk and other leaders say they expect physical bottlenecks, including a shortage of electricity needed to power data centers, to slow down competitors. As utilities warn of multiyear waits for new connections, “speed to power,” or how quickly a data center can get electricity flowing, has become an industry mantra.

The Information editor and writer of The Electric newsletter Steve LeVine moderated a discussion with three leaders pursuing different solutions for smarter architecture, from the grid to the server rack.

  • William Mao, Vice President of Energy Infrastructure, Delta Electronics
  • Allan Schurr, Chief Commercial Officer, ERock
  • Brian Janous, Co-founder, Cloverleaf Infrastructure

The capacity myth

According to Janous, the problem is less about finding gigawatts and more about optimizing them. The grid is underused by about 45% on average, Janous said, because it has to accommodate peaks in usage.

“When a utility says ‘there’s no power for five years,’ what they’re saying is: we don’t have the capacity to meet the coldest winter nights and hottest summer days,” he said, adding that for most hours of the day, there’s enough energy to meet data center needs. (Some notable startups including GridCARE, Emerald AI, Cloverleaf itself as well as Nvidia are trying to figure out how to use such spare capacity.)

Off-grid versus microgrid

Some developers are building their own power plants rather than wait on public utilities’ timelines. But Schurr said going off-grid isn’t necessarily a good long-term solution for data centers.

“It’s a very high-carbon, high-cost commitment,” he said. Instead, he promoted the idea of building a microgrid—a localized power source powered by any number of sources—as a bridge until grid connections arrive. After the data center joins the public grid, the microgrid can still cover peak demand and keep the lights on if the grid goes down.

“It takes three to four years to build a transmission substation,” Schurr said. “We’re building 350 MW microgrid in 16 months.”

Betting on the grid

Cloverleaf looks for sites with spare grid capacity and develops “powered land” around them. Janous said the company has delivered about 7 GW of sites in 18 months, with another 10–12 GW in the pipeline.

Janous agreed with Schurr that going it alone has pitfalls, noting the grid provides services that are hard to replicate, like balancing supply and demand to keep power stable, and restarting the system after a blackout.

“If you have to recreate that behind the meter [in other words, off the public grid,] and think, ‘all I’m doing is building a single power plant,’ you’re in for a rude awakening,” he said.

Simplifying the path to the rack

Mao has watched power infrastructure go from an afterthought to a hot topic.

“For a long time, the electron was not so interesting. Now the space is actually becoming pretty sexy because there’s a lot of demand for the sexy electrons,” he said. That demand puts a spotlight on what happens after power reaches the data center’s door. Delta is tackling that challenge between the grid to the rack.

Mao explained that power typically passes through multiple conversion stages before reaching a server rack. Delta’s solid-state transformers convert medium-voltage AC to the 800-volt DC used by racks in fewer stages, potentially reducing energy losses, as well as reducing the number points of failure.

“Not only do we reduce the number of steps in the distribution chain, but also increase the reliability by removing some of the intermediate power layers,” Mao said.

Solving for AI surges

In the past, data centers traditionally drew steady, predictable power. AI workloads, noted Mao, have changed the game.

“Today with AI, loads no longer measure in kilowatts but in megawatts, and they fluctuate in milliseconds,” he said. Those swings strain the grid.

Managing them takes more sophisticated controls and buffering, he said, adding that Delta’s control platform is built to coordinate different power sources, from the utility grid power, natural gas generation, and to solar and fuel cells. Mao argued that the cleanup should fall to the data center itself, not the utility or its other customers.

Looking ahead, Mao expects the most common setup for large sites to pair natural gas generators with energy storage. Nuclear will play a role too, he said, pointing to a 20-year deal Microsoft signed with Constellation Energy to buy power from a restarted Three Mile Island reactor in Pennsylvania for its data centers.

“You have to have these large blocks of power to move the needle substantially,” he said.

items.title: Encryption Under Siege? OpenAI, Anthropic Disprove Key Cryptography Theorem
items.summary:
Cryptographers who develop encryption technologies may not be sleeping very well these days.

OpenAI and Anthropic both said Monday that their internal AI models had disproven the Exponential Time Hypothesis, a longstanding computer science theorem that predicts the minimum difficulty of solving a certain category of problems. Cryptographers had long assumed the hypothesis was true, and built other findings on the basis of that assumption.

Disproving the Exponential Time Hypothesis won’t endanger any current encryption methods, said Matthew Green, professor of computer science at Johns Hopkins University and founder of encryption startup Zeutro. But the finding is a big theoretical step, showing that some problems are easier to solve than cryptographers had thought.

That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption, a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure.

That means cryptographers could also be wrong about other assumptions underlying core encryption methods such as elliptic curve encryption, a method underlying the majority of internet traffic, which would create a scramble to find new ways to keep information on the internet secure.

items.title: Why Publishers Are Adding Invisible Ads for AI Agents
items.summary:
For as long as there have been ads on the internet, marketing has targeted human eyeballs. But as AI agents crowd onto the web, advertisers and publishers are beginning to deliver ads only AI can see, sparking consternation among some of the agents’ developers, who fear marketers could try to sway agents to take actions without their users’ knowledge.

The first publisher to experiment with these types of invisible ads was venerable Time magazine, which continues to generate a significant portion of its revenue from ads on Time.com. Those ads—for Ally Bank and Project Management Institute, a trade group for project managers—first showed up online in August and were developed in a partnership with Mobian, a New York–based ad tech startup. The ads were designed to give agents information about the institute’s expertise in project management and Ally Bank’s online banking services and ATM network.

Following the ads’ debut, Time has had over 30 meetings with brands about doing similar ads for AI agents, and several new advertisers are launching them now, said Time Chief Operating Officer Mark Howard.

items.title: How Instacart Ended Up in DoorDash’s Cart
items.summary:
That was fast! DoorDash said this morning that it agreed to buy grocery delivery app Instacart for roughly $17 billion, mostly in cash financed by borrowing, just a few days after we reported that Instacart was in talks to sell itself.

After our report, DoorDash and Instacart rushed to seal the deal at a roughly 30% premium to where Instacart shares traded before we broke the news of their talks. They wanted to get it signed before both reported quarterly earnings, which were originally scheduled for next week, say people familiar with the matter. Both companies reported earnings today instead. A deal could take a year or longer to close.  

So how did this deal come together?

Over the years, DoorDash’s leaders have thought about buying Instacart to buttress their grocery sales, according to people familiar with the discussions. Uber, a competitor to DoorDash in restaurant deliveries through Uber Eats, had also talked to Instacart about an acquisition before 2026, and it has had a commercial partnership with Instacart for years. 

Since going public, Instacart’s annual revenue growth has slowed considerably—to 11% in 2025. (In the third quarter, sales increased 17%, according to the earnings report the company released today.) It faces considerable competition from Amazon and Walmart, which both offer grocery deliveries: Walmart accounted for nearly 32% of all online grocery sales in 2025, while Amazon had almost 23%, according to a report from eMarketer, a market research firm. And last year it lost longtime CEO Fidji Simo to OpenAI and Chief Product Officer Daniel Danker to Walmart.

So this year, Instacart’s leaders believed it was the right time to sell, according to people familiar with the matter. 

Instacart leaders also didn’t want to miss a window to merge with a competitor during the Trump administration, which it viewed as being friendlier to such deals, said the people familiar with the deal. 

Around late August, Instacart leaders shopped the company to Uber, according to people familiar with the matter. Uber executives felt obliged to take a look and started talking. Instacart told Uber that it thought a deal could make it past antitrust regulators by arguing that Walmart and Amazon were larger, formidable competitors, according to a person familiar with the pitch. 

Instacart brought on Goldman Sachs, which took Instacart public in 2023, to advise them on a deal. (The grocery delivery firm has long been close to the investment bank, and Goldman partner Nick Giovanni served as Instacart’s chief financial officer from 2021 to 2024.)  

After talking with Uber, Instacart began conversations with DoorDash, people with knowledge of the discussions. Working with boutique bank Centerview Partners, DoorDash sprang to action, the people said. In 2021, DoorDash had considered buying Instacart in a deal that would’ve valued Instacart at more than $40 billion. Nothing happened partly because they thought the acquisition would face antitrust opposition from the Biden administration. While Instacart’s revenue growth has slowed since then, it has started to generate plenty of cash.

Uber wasn’t as keen on a deal. It wasn’t necessarily convinced that regulators would sign off, and it had recently announced another big acquisition, a $15 billion deal for Europe-based Delivery Hero, people close to Uber said. Uber ultimately pulled away from the Instacart talks in September. Instacart then moved ahead with DoorDash. 

A sale to DoorDash could help Instacart compete against Amazon and Walmart by getting in front of relatively well-to-do customers who regularly use the restaurant-delivery app. DoorDash already offers grocery delivery from retailers such as Safeway, in addition to its core restaurant-delivery business. (Some grocers like Kroger already work with both companies, however.)

Research firm Bernstein estimated Tuesday that a combination of DoorDash and Instacart would account for 23% of all online grocery sales in the U.S. 

Wedbush Securities analysts said in a note to investors this week that they expect regulators will be OK with DoorDash buying Instacart. Still, some grocers that work with both companies might not love the deal, so even if U.S. authorities approve it, state attorneys general might review the merger of competitors themselves. 

It isn’t clear what will happen to Instacart’s partnership with Uber, in which customers can order Uber Eats from the Instacart app. But DoorDash said it’s keeping Instacart as a separate brand after the deal closes. 

Apoorva Mehta, the founder of Instacart and its former CEO before Simo joined, said in a statement that he and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu “have explored bringing Instacart and DoorDash together on and off over the years. We kept coming back to it because the industrial logic has always been clear.”

Now that “the biggest companies in the world” are moving deeper into grocery delivery, Mehta says “retailers and restaurants need the technology and service to compete,” and Instacart and DoorDash can be their “partner in that fight.”

items.title: Building a multiplayer game world with autonomous Fable-class models
items.summary:
How I Built the Most AI-Pilled Company in the World

Don't be put off by the clickbait headline, this piece by Jacob Sansbury describing how they are building Spawn is a fascinating exploration of the bleeding edge of what's possible with agentic engineering against frontier models.

Spawn is a massively multiplayer gaming environment where players can use prompts (to the in-game agent, Savi) to modify the game world.

I fired it up on my phone for a few minutes and was able to prompt a castle into existence, then a dragon, then ride the dragon to fly around that castle.

By Jacob's telling, Spawn is now being developed autonomously by a swarm of Fable-powered agents costing over $3 million in tokens per month ("we spend 30x payroll on AI tokens").

Our agents change the live code directly and ship to production hourly, so they read every error, bug report and metric themselves. About 60% of our work starts from a production error, a Savi bug report (Savi is the AI you build games with in Spawn), something odd in our logs, or a feature request.

Savi files bugs herself. When a user hits one, or Savi hits one in the product, she files it. It goes straight to an agent that decides whether it's a real bug to fix, something we won't fix, or intentional design that needs a decision. Usually it becomes a change, delivered to that user within an hour, with a message in the same chat.

This is continuous deployment turned up to 11:

A loop this tight only works if it never stops, so we treat an hour without a ship as a SEV-0, our most severe kind of incident. Unshipped changes pile up, and every problem already in production lasts longer. The feedback slows down too. An agent can only keep a few hours of work in its head, so shipping faster than that actually helps it stay coherent. [...]

We can roll back a broken change in 30 seconds, exactly where it's broken and nowhere else. When a monitor or a log alert fires, it starts or wakes an agent that owns the incident, and we break things on purpose to test that those recovery paths work.

My eyebrows raised at least a dozen times reading this. I have trouble imagining this style of development working on software with higher stakes for when something goes wrong, but for a game this appears to be working surprisingly well.

Jacob says that Fable 5 (and then 5.1) was the model that made this level of autonomy possible. Opus 5.5 doesn't quite hack it for them, and when they tried GPT-6 Astra to apply fixes from a security review everything stopped working:

Every feature had been disabled and marked to be turned on again once the security fixes were done. Astra had gone through our whole product and made the insecure things secure by turning them off.

These kinds of extreme experiments are why I'm excited about game development as a substrate for exploring the edges of what today's coding agents can do.

Tags: game-design, ai, generative-ai, llms, claude, coding-agents, agentic-engineering, claude-mythos-fable

items.title: Quoting Ted Sanders
items.summary:
In general, LLM performance is incredibly multidimensional. There's no guarantee of a fixed ordering where the model that is best at math is also the model that's best at jokes. Despite that complexity, much of the variation in performance is explained by just a single variable: model size. In general, models that are bigger will (a) be more performant / reliable, (b) cost more per token, and (c) have better recall of esoteric facts. As you note, our models are ordered:

Luna < Terra < Sol < Astra

[...] These days, version number signifies a few things at once: the order of release, the relationship to other releases, and the magnitude of improvement. So something like 6.1 would indicate it was launched after 5.6, may share some similarities to other 6.1 models in terms of training data / personality (which is why it's not 5.7), and isn't a giant enough leap to merit the headlines and expectations that would come with a 7.

— Ted Sanders, explaining OpenAI's model naming conventions

Tags: generative-ai, gpt, openai, ai, llms, ted-sanders

items.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026
items.summary:
GitHub Octoverse 2026

I'm at GitHub Universe today (GitHub gave me a free ticket through their "GitHub Stars" program). EVP Jay Parikh just announced this year's Octoverse report, and highlighted these numbers in particular:

This is a pretty stark representation of the impact of agentic engineering on GitHub. In 2026, merged pull requests tripled in less than a year to 220 million per month. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most of that increase in the second half of this year. New repository rate doubled this year, to 30.3 million per month.

The report includes new numbers by industry, and breaks out numbers for repositories that involve "interoperability or reverse engineering". The methodology section includes notes about how they did this:

Top countries by pushes to public repositories, adjusted by profile location. Pushes from each country were summed across the Octoverse year. To adjust for biases caused by VPN usage, LLM classification was used to extract the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code from the profiles of GitHub users who contributed pushes during this period [...]

Industry. Public repositories created 2022 to 2026 were sorted into NAICS sectors by a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model using name, description, topics, and README, from random samples per year. [...]

Interoperability. Counts public repositories created each year whose name, description, topics, or README mention interoperability or reverse engineering, or related terms, such as clean room implementation, drop-in replacement, or protocol re-implementation.

Tags: github, ai, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, disclosures, agentic-engineering

items.title: The October inflection point for vibe game development
items.summary:
I've written before about how November 2025 was an inflection point for coding agents - the point where Opus 4.5 and GPT-5.1 crossed a tipping point that meant their respective coding agents became reliable daily drivers for software engineers. I think we've reached a new inflection point in October 2026, and this time it's for vibe coding computer games.

  • Tree Appreciator
  • Emberwick
  • Battle Drones
  • Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
  • Four times as insulting
  • What happens if someone actually puts the work in?
  • You should build a game!

Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

  • 3D modeling
  • Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox)
  • Game design (!)

That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play.

Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it.

Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did.

In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing.

I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance.

I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.

Tree Appreciator

The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator. I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code.

I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here. Here's the chat transcript that built it.

It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.

Emberwick

This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:

Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening

Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great

Here's that first version. It worked really well!

I was inspired to increase my ambitions:

Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that

Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village

Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll

Here's that version.

When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:

Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good

We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.

Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.

Here's that final game. It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.

There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.

Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave".

Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.

I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well.

Battle Drones

This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week. It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.

This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is.

The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play.

I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up.

Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules.

It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna:

Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game.

I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache (screenshots here), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!

Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove

I live in Half Moon Bay, California, home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival, which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.

I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.

I called it "Quarter Sun Cove".

I'm still iterating on this project, but it's shaping up quite nicely. It's a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.

Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.

It's absurdly cute.

You can play the latest version here. I'm not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it's actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.

Here's the initial brainstorming session, which resulted in this spec file. Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.

I told Claude to "surprise and delight the user frequently" and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.

This isn't my best game yet - it's not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn't have been built in the before-times.

Four times as insulting

If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once.

I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself.

The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve's Steam Next Fest is a good recent example.

We now have games where everything - code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself - can be outsourced to the models. And the results don't suck!

Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone!

I expect that, as we've already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction!

I certainly won't be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions - I don't feel like I've earned that right. We'll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects.

What happens if someone actually puts the work in?

The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input. The projects I've described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I've put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself).

Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it's as good as they can make it.

I want to see games that wouldn't have existed without these new tools.

You should build a game!

Building games in this way is so much fun. It's the perfect application for vibe coding because it's so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project?

(OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache!)

All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages). Modern browsers - including mobile browsers - are incredibly capable. Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser. I'm finding these mobile web games to be indistinguishable from the native experience, at least for the kinds of games I'm trying to build.

I suggest starting with a prompt like this:

Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where...

This works on both chatgpt.com and claude.ai - you don't even need to fire up a full coding agent. As one last example, here's "Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where a mouse has to hide from a cat" by Claude Opus 5.5 Extra and by GPT-6 Extra High.

Switch to Codex or Claude Code once your project passes the proof-of-concept phase.

And if the game isn't fun enough, add this:

Make it a LOT more fun

  • Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove
  • Four times as insulting
  • What happens if someone actually puts the work in?
  • You should build a game!

Claude Opus 5.5 in particular exhibits meaningful improvements in several areas needed to build a compelling game:

  • 3D modeling
  • Music generation (see Scrimshaw Jukebox)
  • Game design (!)

That last one is particularly important. Models have been able to create something that looks like a game for quite a while now, as seen in my previous experiments. The challenge has been getting to a game that's actually fun to play.

Game design is a deep subject area. I won't pretend to be well versed in it - I know enough to have respect for it as a craft. Creating a novel, compelling gameplay loop which challenges players at the right level and provides a satisfying learning curve is a fine art. I didn't think the models could do it.

Then I tried telling Claude Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun"... and it did.

In the past few weeks I've vibe coded (in the classic sense of the term - no looking at the code at all) four games that I've genuinely enjoyed playing.

I attended Foo Camp in Berkeley over the weekend and met several people who were having similar experiences. Building games that play well is shockingly easy now. The new challenge is coming up with concepts for games that are novel and delightful and that wouldn't exist without AI assistance.

I haven't done an exhaustive study, but my current impression is that GPT-6 Astra isn't quite there yet. It can absolutely build a game, but its sense of fun doesn't match that of Opus 5.5. I expect OpenAI will get there by the end of the year.

Here are the four game projects that have convinced me that the models are now capable of producing fun games with very little guidance. All four are built in HTML and JavaScript and run entirely in the browser.

Tree Appreciator

The smallest game I found to be genuinely delightful is Tree Appreciator. I used the regular Claude chat interface for this - it didn't even need Claude Code.

I built this on a whim while we were driving along Skyline Boulevard looking at trees. My prompt was:

Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful.

I've found that telling models to use three.js works really well. Claude doesn't have its own image generation model but is capable of building full-color 3D models that look and feel excellent.

This game required no iteration or follow-up prompting at all - I got the game in a single shot. It gave me back a charming little mobile-friendly spot-the-difference game. You can play that here. Here's the chat transcript that built it.

It's pleasingly relaxing. The graphics are fun, and collecting trees that you have completed in a "herbarium" provides a nice, cosy sense of accomplishment.

Emberwick

This was a more ambitious project that I again built using regular Claude chat. I started out by building an experimental prototype of an engine for a top-down fantasy RPG:

Build a demo game engine three.js which is a top down (but at an angle) RPG - the player gets to move through the world with one or two companions. Create a fantasy village setting that demonstrates walking around outside and then shows how when the player enters a building the wall between the player and the camera goes transparent so the user can see what is happening

Add some NPCs and plenty of furniture and different types of building some with an upstairs - be creative, make it look great

Here's that first version. It worked really well!

I was inspired to increase my ambitions:

Make it not so flat - the buildings are great but the landscape itself is completely flat at the moment, fix that

Add basements to two of the buildings with a tunnel system joining them below the village

Add the start of a rocky mountain on one side of the village containing a cave with a sleeping troll

Here's that version.

When that produced a good result, I decided to push it all the way:

Now turn this into an actual game - quadruple the size of the playable area, introduce fun game mechanics, add a plot that isn't too cliche, some twists, a magic system, make it really good

We're back to prompts like "make it really good" here! Asking for a plot that "isn't too cliche" seemed to work too - it's a bit cliché, but still novel enough that I enjoyed following the story.

Unlike Tree Appreciator, this took quite a bit of additional playtesting and prompting to get to a finished version. This was mainly due to gameplay problems - things like a character not being in the right place to complete a quest because a different story element had caused them to move to another location.

Here's that final game. It has a full story that takes about 15 minutes to play through.

There's even an experimental level editor if you want to drop in your own houses, furniture, and landscape features.

Once it was all working (and I'd iterated through some gameplay bugs), I played it through from start to finish and found myself emotionally affected by the ending! I'm somewhat embarrassed by this, because everything in this game - the graphics, the plot, the characters, the music, the dialog - came from the model. My creative input was pretty much just "it's a fantasy village and there's a troll asleep in a cave".

Here's the full shared Claude chat in which I built this game.

I also fed that same initial sequence of prompts through ChatGPT GPT-6 Pro. Here's the transcript and the finished game for comparison. It looks great, but I don't think it plays nearly as well.

Battle Drones

This is by far my most successful project, which I wrote about last week. It's a Command & Conquer-style Real-Time Strategy game where two robot armies (or four as of Saturday) build units, harvest scrap, and battle over territory.

This is also the project that convinced me that Opus 5.5 knows what "fun" is.

The first versions were built back in July using Claude Fable 5. It got me to a workable 2D Command & Conquer-style game, but it wasn't great to play.

I prompted Opus 5.5 to "Make it a LOT more fun" and then later to "Port this game to three.js" and the game was transformed. There's a blow-by-blow account (prompts included) in my write-up.

Today, Battle Drones has 2-4 player multiplayer (via a vibe coded WebSockets relay server), medals, replays, seven maps, a random map generator, and a set of "mutators" that add variants of the rules.

It also lets different LLMs play against each other, using a mode where the game advances five seconds and then pauses to give different models time to interpret the new game state and line up their next set of commands. Here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna:

Battle Drones is a particularly good example of Opus 5.5's ability to create 3D models. This page lets you browse all of the models in the game.

I released Battle Drones under the Apache 2.0 License last Tuesday. On Wednesday Gabriel Turpin released Panache (screenshots here), a fork of Battle Drones that reimagined the game for steampunk 1900s Belle Époque France, with new models and music and an animated intro sequence. Open source at work!

Pumpkin Farmer, aka Quarter Sun Cove

I live in Half Moon Bay, California, home of the annual Half Moon Bay Art and Pumpkin Festival, which includes a giant pumpkin weigh-off competition.

I decided to try building a game that wasn't just a cheap imitation of something that already existed, so I set out to create a game about farming pumpkins, growing giant pumpkins, and handling the rush of the October pumpkin season.

I called it "Quarter Sun Cove".

I'm still iterating on this project, but it's shaping up quite nicely. It's a cosy farming simulator where you spend the year tending to your giant pumpkin and planting out regular-sized pumpkins for sale in October, then sell pumpkins during pumpkin season and enter your giant pumpkin in the weigh-off.

Every character in it is a (vegetarian) animal. The mayor of the town is a pelican. You can be a pelican, skunk, raccoon, possum, beaver, coyote, fox, owl, sea otter, or harbor seal. Those species all later show up (accompanied by their children) to buy pumpkins from you.

It's absurdly cute.

You can play the latest version here. I'm not convinced by the game mechanics yet - it's actually quite complicated: you have to decide when to plant pumpkins such that they will become ripe at the weekends in October with the most visitors.

Here's the initial brainstorming session, which resulted in this spec file. Then I had Opus 5.5 Ultracode burn millions of tokens and nearly two days building it.

I told Claude to "surprise and delight the user frequently" and the result is so many little details and easter eggs. There are mischievous raccoons, an elephant seal that runs the weigh-off, harbor seals that roll their pumpkins back into the ocean, a wandering goat, and superstitions about growing giant pumpkins that sometimes come true.

This isn't my best game yet - it's not as fun to play as Battle Drones - but it represents the kind of game I want more of: weird, fun, uniquely personal - something that wouldn't have been built in the before-times.

Four times as insulting

If you are offended by AI-generated art, AI-generated music, AI-generated writing, and AI-generated code, I have bad news for you: vibe coded games combine all of those at once.

I respect those opinions, even though I don’t strongly hold them myself.

The wider games community already has an aversion to AI-generated assets in games. This has been a growing issue over the past few years as tools like Midjourney have enabled developers to generate assets for their projects. This IGN story covering complaints about slop in Valve's Steam Next Fest is a good recent example.

We now have games where everything - code, assets, dialog, and even the game design itself - can be outsourced to the models. And the results don't suck!

Building a computer game used to be one of the most challenging projects in all of software development, combining a diverse range of skills and requiring intense focus and effort over many months or even years. And now here I am spitting out a playable multiplayer RTS by prompting on my phone!

I expect that, as we've already seen with programming, this will result in a split. Some players will refuse to have anything to do with games that were built in this way. Others may embrace this as opening up game development to a much wider audience. I lean in that direction!

I certainly won't be entering any of my vibe coded games in traditional game jams or competitions - I don't feel like I've earned that right. We'll likely see new avenues emerge for vibe game developers to compare their projects.

What happens if someone actually puts the work in?

The thing I find both exciting and shameful about this is that I have got interesting results from so little creative input. The projects I've described here are loosely ordered by how much effort I've put into them. Not a single project represents more than four hours of my work (plus many more hours of Claude Code churning away by itself).

Now imagine what could be achieved by anyone who takes this seriously, invests significant creative time, applies better taste in game design, and then playtests and iterates on the result until it's as good as they can make it.

I want to see games that wouldn't have existed without these new tools.

You should build a game!

Building games in this way is so much fun. It's the perfect application for vibe coding because it's so low stakes: how much damage can you cause with a bug in a personal vibe coded game project?

(OK, you can do some damage... my attempt at audio-based multiplayer gave my wife Natalie a nasty headache!)

All of my games so far have been HTML and JavaScript using static hosting (generally GitHub Pages or Cloudflare Pages). Modern browsers - including mobile browsers - are incredibly capable. Frontier models already know libraries like three.js and Phaser. I'm finding these mobile web games to be indistinguishable from the native experience, at least for the kinds of games I'm trying to build.

I suggest starting with a prompt like this:

Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where...

This works on both chatgpt.com and claude.ai - you don't even need to fire up a full coding agent. As one last example, here's "Build a mobile-friendly three.js game where a mouse has to hide from a cat" by Claude Opus 5.5 Extra and by GPT-6 Extra High.

Switch to Codex or Claude Code once your project passes the proof-of-concept phase.

And if the game isn't fun enough, add this:

Make it a LOT more fun

items.title: Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge

Game Boy Color on My Conference Badge

I'm at GitHub Universe this week and, similar to last year, the conference badge is a full-blown color screen computer.

I've been hacking around with it again, and then I ran into with Steve Francia... who worked with Gemini to get a full NES emulator working on it, and then went a step further and deployed an emulator for both the Game Boy and the Game Boy Color.

A neat feature of the badge is that you can turn it upside down and then use game controller touch buttons that are built into the badge body.
